newsitem.title: USA: AT&T's talks with SBC cool, sources say.
newsitem.headline: AT&T's talks with SBC cool, sources say.

text.p: Merger talks between AT&T Corp. and SBC Communications Inc. have cooled, sources close to the discussions said Friday, putting on hold, perhaps for good, what would have been the largest merger in history.

The unwinding of the potential $50 billion deal is likely to refocus attention on AT&T's efforts to boost its long-distance business and casts a harsh light on the weakness of its efforts to enter U.S. local phone markets.
Sources close to the discussions, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed a report in Friday's Wall Street Journal that the talks were on hold but declined to provide details.

Analysts said the deal -- which from the outset was given long odds of winning regulatory approval -- appears to have run aground because of unexpectedly stiff resistance from Washington regulators and widespread public criticism.

Last week, outgoing Federal Communications Commission chief Reed Hundt called the merger "unthinkable," as he sought to draw a halt to such mega-mergers in general and any deal between AT&T and a regional Bell phone company in particular.

The two companies declined to comment Friday on the status of any merger talks that may have occurred between them, despite AT&T Chairman Robert Allen's public campaign to win support for the idea of a Baby Bell merger.
"I don't think AT&T ever imagined that there would be such vehement opposition," said Jeffrey Kagan, an industry consultant. "They were in denial," he said.

"This was like trying to put lipstick on a rhino," agreed Scott Cleland, director of brokerage Legg Mason's regulatory research group. "They were trying to dress up to make the deal presentable ... but in the past few weeks, reality set in."
AT&T is the nation's leading long-distance carrier with about 60 percent of the market. SBC offers local phone services in seven states stretching from Texas to California.

A deal involving the two was hampered by federal laws that prohibit Baby Bells such as SBC from offering long-distance services in their home region until they can satisfy a list of regulatory requirements designed to open their markets to greater competition.
Kagan, who heads Kagan Telecom Associates in Atlanta, saw AT&T's desire to pair with a regional Bell local service provider as inviting a battle with antitrust regulators.

By contrast, rivals such as MCI Communications Corp. and Sprint Corp. have managed to avoid such conflicts by teaming up with European partners, Kagan said. "AT&T was looking for a quick fix," he said.

Cleland said the impact of the failed merger will be felt largely by AT&T, not SBC. "It signals that AT&T wanted to rush to the end game of deregulating markets to promote wider competition," he said.
"They didn't see a good way to replicate the local loop so they wanted to buy it," Cleland said of AT&T's apparent desire to gain a foothold in SBC's local phone region.
While the deal appears to have hit a brick wall for now, analysts said they would not foreclose new efforts by AT&T to combine with another Baby Bell or even SBC.
"We can say this deal is unravelling, but does that mean it is dead? No way," Kagan said of the AT&T-SBC talks.
"These talks between AT&T and everyone else are fluid and have been going on for years," he said. "This deal appears to be cooling down, but there is always an ebb and flow to these discussions."

"The cows are out of the barn," industry cosultant Bill Bane said of the growing trends toward consolidation in telecommunications. "It is clear that there will be mergers like this in the next few years."
AT&T stock fell 31 cents to $35.81 and SBC lost 19 cents to $59.94, both in composite trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
